title: Emergency Approach & Landing

required_knowledge_points.title: Engine Failure — Aviate First, Memory Items, and the 91.3 Emergency Authority
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE kills your engine on the checkride. Your FIRST action tells them everything. If you look down at the panel, you fail. If you pitch for best glide FIRST, you pass. The pilot who troubleshoots before flying will stall the aircraft. Aviate → Navigate → Communicate → Troubleshoot.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: ENGINE FAILURE PRIORITY: AVIATE FIRST. The instant the engine fails, the aircraft begins decelerating due to parasitic and induced drag. If the pilot does not IMMEDIATELY pitch for best glide (Vg), the aircraft decelerates through the stall. This is the #1 cause of death in engine-failure accidents — not the engine failure itself, but the stall that follows when the pilot troubleshoots instead of flying. MEMORY ITEMS vs. CHECKLISTS: Memory items are rote-memorized immediate actions for time-critical emergencies (Pitch for Vg → Fuel Selector BOTH → Mixture RICH → Carb Heat ON → Magnetos BOTH → Primer IN AND LOCKED). These are performed from MUSCLE MEMORY because the pilot's cognitive load under acute stress cannot process reading tasks while managing the aircraft. After memory items are complete and the aircraft is stabilized: transition to the PRINTED checklist. The printed checklist contains secondary items the stressed brain will skip: unlatch cabin doors before touchdown (prevents frame warping and trapping occupants), secure the electrical system (prevents post-crash fire), squawk 7700, transmit on 121.5. 14 CFR 91.3(b): in an emergency requiring immediate action, the PIC may deviate from ANY rule to meet the emergency. This includes: violating airspace, landing on highways, deviating from ATC clearances. The FAA will review the deviation after the fact — but survival comes first.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Engine Failure — First 10 Seconds
```
1. PITCH for Vg (best glide) ← THE most important action
2. Select a landing field
3. Run memory items:
   Fuel Selector → BOTH
   Mixture → RICH
   Carb Heat → ON
   Magnetos → BOTH
   Primer → IN AND LOCKED
4. TRIM for Vg (hands-off stabilization)
5. Transition to PRINTED checklist
```

### Memory Items vs. Printed Checklists
| Type | When | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Memory items** | Immediately, from muscle memory | Stress destroys working memory — can't read under acute load |
| **Printed checklist** | After aircraft stabilized | Catches items the stressed brain skips (doors, electrical, comms) |

### Commonly Missed Checklist Items
- ❌ Unlatch cabin doors before touchdown (frame warps on impact = trapped)
- ❌ Secure electrical system (prevents post-crash fire)
- ❌ Squawk 7700 + transmit 121.5
- ❌ ELT activation check

### 14 CFR 91.3(b) — Emergency Authority
- PIC may deviate from **ANY** regulation to meet the emergency
- Includes: airspace violations, unauthorized landings, ATC deviations
- FAA reviews after — survival comes first

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** If the DPE pulls your throttle and you look DOWN at the panel first, you have failed. Your FIRST action is PITCH FOR Vg. Always.

required_knowledge_points.title: Best Glide vs. Minimum Sink — When to Use Each and Why Weight Matters
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'What is the difference between best glide speed and minimum sink speed?' Best glide = maximum DISTANCE. Minimum sink = maximum TIME. If the field is far away, fly Vg. If you're troubleshooting over a lake, fly minimum sink. And Vg DECREASES as the aircraft gets lighter — most pilots don't know this.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: BEST GLIDE SPEED (Vg): occurs at L/D max — the airspeed where total drag (parasite + induced) is at its minimum. Provides the FLATTEST glide angle and maximum ground distance per foot of altitude lost. Use Vg when: the objective is to REACH a distant landing site. MINIMUM SINK SPEED (Vms): found at the lowest point on the power-required curve, approximately 5-10 knots SLOWER than Vg. Provides the LOWEST vertical descent rate (e.g., 500 fpm vs. 700 fpm at Vg). Use minimum sink when: the objective is to STAY AIRBORNE as long as possible — troubleshooting over a specific area, ditching preparation, or waiting for rescue coordination. Minimum sink is CLOSER to the critical AOA than Vg — smaller margin to stall. WEIGHT EFFECT ON Vg: the published Vg is calculated at MAXIMUM GROSS WEIGHT. A lighter aircraft requires less lift → generates less induced drag → optimal L/D max occurs at a LOWER airspeed. Rule of thumb: Vg decreases ~1% for every 2% below max gross weight. WIND EFFECTS ON GLIDE RANGE: Headwind = reduces ground distance at Vg. To maximize ground range into a headwind, fly FASTER than Vg (increases ground speed, reduces time in the headwind). Tailwind = increases ground distance. Fly SLIGHTLY SLOWER than Vg to maximize the tailwind benefit. THE 'STRETCHING THE GLIDE' FALLACY: pulling back to fly SLOWER than Vg increases induced drag, STEEPENS the descent angle, and DECREASES ground distance. The pilot lands even shorter than if they had maintained Vg.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Best Glide vs. Minimum Sink
| Parameter | Best Glide (Vg) | Minimum Sink (Vms) |
|---|---|---|
| **Objective** | Maximum DISTANCE | Maximum TIME aloft |
| **Aerodynamic point** | L/D max | Bottom of power-required curve |
| **Speed relative to each other** | Faster | ~5-10 kts slower |
| **Stall margin** | Larger | Smaller (closer to critical AOA) |
| **Use when** | Need to REACH a field | Need to STAY AIRBORNE |

### Weight Effect on Vg
- Published Vg = at **max gross weight**
- Lighter aircraft = less lift needed = less induced drag
- Optimal Vg **decreases** as weight decreases
- Rule of thumb: ~1% Vg decrease per 2% weight decrease

### Wind Corrections
| Wind | Correction | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Headwind** | Fly **faster** than Vg | Reduces time in headwind → more ground distance |
| **Tailwind** | Fly **slightly slower** than Vg | Maximizes tailwind benefit |
| **No wind** | Fly **exactly** Vg | Standard L/D max performance |

### The Trim Imperative
- Trim for Vg → aircraft maintains speed **hands-off**
- Frees hands for checklists, radios, field selection
- Without trim: pilot fights controls → cognitive overload → stall

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** 'Does Vg change with weight?' YES — it decreases as the aircraft gets lighter. Most pilots quote the published Vg without understanding it's calculated at max gross.

required_knowledge_points.title: Emergency Landing Strategy — Energy Management, Key Positions, and the Impossible Turn
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'How do you plan an emergency landing without an engine?' The answer is energy management. You can only SPEND energy (altitude and airspeed) — you can't create it. The strategy: stay HIGH, fly the key positions, and only add drag (flaps) when the field is ASSURED. And the impossible turn? Below your pre-briefed turnback altitude, you land STRAIGHT AHEAD.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: ENERGY MANAGEMENT: in an unpowered aircraft, total energy = potential (altitude) + kinetic (airspeed). You cannot create energy without an engine. Drag is a constant tax bleeding energy away. Key principle: it is always better to arrive TOO HIGH than too low. Excess altitude can be shed (slips, S-turns, flaps). An altitude DEFICIT is unrecoverable. CONFIGURATION TIMING: flaps and gear are IRREVERSIBLE energy expenditures. Deploying flaps steepens the descent dramatically. Deploy flaps ONLY when the field is absolutely assured and excess energy must be shed. Premature flap deployment = landing short. Retracting flaps after deployment = sudden lift loss + altitude loss. KEY POSITION METHODOLOGY: adapted from military/glider pilots. High Key = 1,500 ft AGL over the intended touchdown point. Fly a continuous spiraling pattern. Low Key = 800 ft AGL abeam the touchdown point. This creates standardized visual references — the pilot can intuitively assess if they're high or low and adjust turns accordingly. THE IMPOSSIBLE TURN: after an engine failure on takeoff, the reflexive instinct is to turn back to the runway. Physics: a 180° turn (actually ~210° to realign with the runway) requires bank → increased load factor → increased stall speed → increased descent rate. Below the pre-calculated turnback altitude (varies by aircraft, typically 800-1,200 ft AGL), the turn back GUARANTEES a low-altitude stall/spin. Pre-takeoff briefing: 'If the engine fails below [X] feet, I will land STRAIGHT AHEAD within 30° of the nose.' CONE OF SAFETY: the pilot should maintain continuous awareness of the gliding radius available from current altitude. Over hostile terrain (mountains, forests, water), climb higher to expand the cone.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Energy Management — The Closed System
```
Total Energy = Altitude (potential) + Airspeed (kinetic)
```
- **Cannot create energy** without an engine
- **Can only spend it** — drag bleeds it away continuously
- **Golden rule:** arrive TOO HIGH, never too low
- Too high → shed energy (slips, S-turns, flaps)
- Too low → **unrecoverable** — no fix exists

### Configuration Timing
| When | Flaps |
|---|---|
| Field NOT assured | **Clean** — maximize glide |
| Field assured, excess energy | **Deploy incrementally** — shed energy |
| Landing short | **DO NOT retract** — sudden lift loss = crash |

### Key Position Methodology
| Position | Altitude (AGL) | Location |
|---|---|---|
| **High Key** | ~1,500 ft | Over the touchdown point |
| **Low Key** | ~800 ft | Abeam the touchdown point |
| **Base Key** | ~500 ft | Turning base |

### The Impossible Turn
```
Engine failure on takeoff → instinct says "turn back to runway"
→ 210° of turn → bank → load factor → stall speed increases
→ Below turnback altitude → GUARANTEED low-altitude stall/spin
→ FATAL
```
**Pre-takeoff briefing:** "Below [X] feet, I land STRAIGHT AHEAD within 30° of the nose."

### Field Selection Priorities
1. Aim for **upwind side** of field (shortest ground roll)
2. Look for **poles** (wires are invisible — poles aren't)
3. Align with **furrows/crop lines** (prevent gear dig-in and flip)
4. Prefer **cultivated fields** over paved roads (no traffic, no wires)

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** 'Your engine fails at 400 feet after takeoff. Do you turn back?' NO. 400 feet is below any safe turnback altitude. Land STRAIGHT AHEAD.

lesson_overview:
## Emergency Approach and Landing — Energy Management Without an Engine

This lesson covers the most critical emergency in single-engine flying: the complete loss of engine power and the subsequent forced landing. This is the scenario the DPE will simulate on every private pilot checkride, and the pilot's response in the first 10 seconds determines whether the outcome is survivable.

**The instant the engine fails, the aircraft becomes an unpowered glider with a fixed, finite energy budget.** The pilot's first action — before any troubleshooting, before any radio call, before any checklist — is to pitch for best glide speed (Vg). This single action preserves the kinetic energy required to maintain flight control and maximizes the distance the aircraft can travel to reach a suitable landing site. The pilot who looks down at the instrument panel to troubleshoot before pitching for Vg will stall the aircraft as airspeed decays — and the stall, not the engine failure, is what kills. Memory items follow: fuel selector, mixture, carb heat, magnetos, primer. These are performed from muscle memory because the brain's cognitive capacity under acute stress cannot process reading tasks. Only after the aircraft is aerodynamically stabilized does the pilot transition to the printed checklist, which contains the secondary items that the stressed brain invariably skips: unlatching doors, securing electrical systems, squawking 7700.

**Best glide speed and minimum sink speed serve fundamentally different objectives.** Best glide occurs at L/D max — the airspeed where total drag is minimized — and provides the greatest forward distance for each foot of altitude lost. Minimum sink speed is approximately 5-10 knots slower and provides the lowest vertical descent rate, keeping the aircraft airborne for the longest possible time. The choice between them depends entirely on the objective: reaching a distant field demands Vg; troubleshooting over a specific area or preparing for a water ditching demands minimum sink. A critical detail most pilots miss: the published Vg is calculated at maximum gross weight. A lighter aircraft achieves its best glide ratio at a lower airspeed because less lift is required, generating less induced drag.

**The emergency landing itself is an exercise in energy management and geometric planning.** The pilot cannot create energy without an engine — they can only spend it. Drag is a constant tax. The golden rule is to arrive intentionally high: excess altitude can always be shed through slips, S-turns, or flap deployment. An altitude deficit is unrecoverable. The Key Position methodology provides a standardized visual framework: High Key at 1,500 feet AGL over the touchdown point, Low Key at 800 feet AGL abeam. Flaps are deployed only when the field is absolutely assured — premature deployment steepens the descent and guarantees landing short. And the impossible turn — the reflexive instinct to turn back to the departure runway — is a mathematical death trap below the pre-calculated turnback altitude. The physics of banked flight increase stall speed and descent rate, and below 800-1,200 feet AGL, the turn back guarantees a low-altitude stall or spin.
